title: How Do You Structure a Voice of Customer Team? The Roles You Need and How Many People
summary: A VoC team needs five jobs, not five people: program owner, analyst, taxonomy owner, stakeholder partner and data. One to three people can cover them.
body_markdown:
Most voice of customer (VoC) and customer experience (CX) measurement teams are small and asked to cover a lot. Forrester's 2024 report on the subject is titled["Stretched Thin: VoC And CX Measurement Teams Struggle For Resources,"](https://www.forrester.com/report/stretched-thin-voc-and-cx-measurement-teams-struggle-for-resources/RES180657) and describes these teams as "small and often tasked with covering the entire organization." Forrester research[reported by DestinationCRM](https://www.destinationcrm.com/Articles/CRM-Insights/Insight/Companies-Need-to-Do-More-CX-and-VoC-Measurement-157479.aspx) in 2023 found that 56% of these teams have three people or fewer.


Structure the team around jobs, not job titles. A VoC program needs five jobs done: a program owner, an analyst, a taxonomy owner, a stakeholder partner, and someone who owns data and integrations. At smaller scale, one to three people cover all five. Feedback analytics software like Thematic now handles much of the repetitive work inside those jobs (coding comments into themes, keeping themes current, drafting summaries and sending scheduled reports), so the people you hire spend their time on judgment.


Below is a five-step way to build or resize the team, a worked example, and the mistakes to avoid.


## The 5-step process


1. **List the five jobs** a VoC program needs, whoever does them.
2. **Decide where the team sits** : one central team, or a central team with partners in each business unit.
3. **Combine the jobs to fit your headcount** , whether that's one, two or three people.
4. **Move the repetitive work to software** so people keep the judgment calls.
5. **Add people when specific triggers hit** , not when the backlog feels heavy.


## Step 1: List the five jobs


Every VoC program does the same five jobs, even when one person does all of them.


Job What it covers What software can take What stays human


Program owner Goals, budget, executive sponsor, deciding what gets measured Little All of it


Analyst Reading feedback, finding drivers, answering questions Coding comments into themes, first-pass summaries Interpreting results and checking them against the comments


Taxonomy owner Keeping themes accurate and consistent across sources Spotting new phrases and suggesting new themes Approving changes and defining what each theme means


Stakeholder partner Getting product, operations and frontline teams to act Scheduled reports and alerts Relationships, follow-up, closing the loop


Data and integrations Connecting survey, support and review sources Scheduled data pulls once connected Choosing sources and fixing data quality


The Customer Experience Professionals Association (CXPA) gives the analyst seat a stakeholder duty as well: it "Ensures stakeholders understand how to interpret and apply VOC data." That's a reminder the analyst and stakeholder jobs overlap more than an org chart suggests.


## Step 2: Decide where the team sits


Most large companies centralize. In XM Institute's 2023 survey of companies with 1,000 or more employees, "Seventy-eight percent have a centralized customer experience team."[McKinsey suggests in a 2016 article](https://karriere.mckinsey.de/capabilities/operations/our-insights/leading-and-governing-the-customer-centric-organization) that "a permanent customer-experience team of 2 to 20 members is usually sufficient, regardless of company size."


A central team works when one group can own the program end to end. Once several business units each need their own answers, add a partner in each unit. XM Institute calls this a federated model: "a structure for enabling and coordinating a distributed set of customer experience capabilities." The central team keeps the taxonomy and the standards. Business-unit partners own action in their area.


For more on who should own VoC across the company, see[Who owns voice of the customer?](https://getthematic.com/insights/who-owns-voice-of-the-customer) .


## Step 3: Combine the jobs to fit your headcount


Most teams can't hire five people for five jobs. Combine them like this:


- **One person:** owns the program, analyzes and keeps the taxonomy. Stakeholder partnering is shared with one champion in each team that receives reports. Data connections are set up once with IT or the vendor.
- **Two people:** a program owner who also partners with stakeholders, and an analyst who also owns the[taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) and data connections.
- **Three people:** a program owner, an analyst, and an insights partner who works with business units and keeps the taxonomy.


Whichever version you pick, write down who owns each job. A program where one person holds everything in their head is fragile.[What happens when the person who built your feedback program leaves](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-program-owner-leaves) covers how to protect against that.


## Step 4: Move the repetitive work to software


Repetitive work fills a small team's week.[Forrester's 2025 survey of feedback programs](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/feedback-and-cx-measurement-programs-must-boost-their-impact-according-to-forresters-2025-survey/) found that "Over half of programs already see value in genAI for summarizing feedback." It also found "Less than 1/3 (27%) effectively communicate insights in a timely way."


In Thematic, much of the repetitive work in the five jobs is automated:


- **Coding comments:** Thematic creates themes from open-ended feedback using AI, and people refine them in the theme editor.
- **Keeping themes current:** Theme Maintenance can check a lens's feedback each month, add new phrases to existing themes and suggest new themes for review. Nothing changes until someone approves it.
- **First-pass summaries:** generative AI summaries are available in the analysis tools and as dashboard widgets.
- **Reporting:** dashboards can be[emailed on a schedule](https://getthematic.com/insights/automate-customer-feedback-reporting) , and workflows send alerts to email or Slack.
- **Data:** connectors pull feedback from sources such as Qualtrics, Zendesk and Intercom on a set cadence.


The human jobs that remain are approving theme changes, interpreting results and getting teams to act. Those are the jobs worth hiring for.


## Step 5: Add people when specific triggers hit


Add a person when one of these happens, not when the team simply feels busy:


- **A new business unit needs its own answers** and has nobody to partner with.
- **Questions wait more than a week** for an answer, even with summaries and dashboards in place.
- **Theme changes pile up unreviewed** because nobody has time to own the taxonomy.
- **Insights reach stakeholders but nothing changes** , which means the stakeholder partner job is uncovered.


Each trigger points to the job that needs more time, so you know which role to hire.


## What does this look like in practice?


[Mitre10](https://getthematic.com/insights/humanising-hardware-how-mitre10-made-voice-of-customer-actionable-with-thematic) , a cooperative retail business with stores across New Zealand, ran its program with a small three-person insights team. That team handled 20,000 verbatim comments a month across 84 stores. With Thematic, the team found that stock availability issues were taking half a net promoter score (NPS) point off overall scores. In Mitre10's words, the team could "spend our time working with the data, not on it."


[Community Health System](https://getthematic.com/insights/community-health-systems-actionable-insights) , a not-for-profit healthcare network in California's central San Joaquin Valley, shows the time this frees up. For its employee engagement survey, preparation dropped from about an hour to about 20 minutes per department. That saved more than 160 hours per survey cycle and let the team produce 250 one-page department reports in three days.


In both cases, software took on the coding and reporting work, and the people kept the decisions.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Hiring by title, not by job.** List the five jobs first, then decide who covers each.
- **Leaving the taxonomy unowned.** Name one person who approves theme changes.
- **Treating stakeholder work as optional.** Forrester's 2025 research says most programs still struggle to get stakeholders to act on CX insights.
- **Hiring analysts to code comments by hand.** Use software for coding and hire for interpretation.
- **Keeping the program in one person's head.** Write down who owns each job and how the taxonomy is defined.
- **Growing headcount with volume.** Add people when a specific trigger shows a job is uncovered.
